Radical scavenger experiments indicated a greater contribution of radical species in the Fe-containing materials, whereas NiAl-LDH showed a more adsorption-driven removal pathway. No synergistic enhancement between Ni and Fe was observed, as NiAl-LDH exhibited comparable or superior performance despite containing the non-redox-active Al3+ center. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that Ni centers play a dominant role in persulfate activation, whereas the trivalent metal primarily modulates the electronic structure and the reaction pathway of the catalyst. These findings challenge the conventional assumption that the presence of multiple redox-active metal centers necessarily enhances the catalytic performance in LDH systems and highlight the critical role of the local electronic environment in designing efficient catalysts for environmental applications.

item.title: Temperature-Dependent Enzyme-Ligand Recognition Emerges from the Coupling of Protein Dynamics and Hydration
item.description:
Abstract
Protein–ligand interactions are governed by a subtle interplay between binding thermodynamics, protein dynamics, and hydration. However, how these factors are coupled remains poorly understood, particularly for enzymes whose function depends on coordinated water rearrangements. Here, we investigate the binding of the fluorinated sulfonamide inhibitors 4-fluorobenzenesulfonamide (4FBS) and pentafluorobenzenesulfonamide (PFBS) to the zinc metalloenzyme bovine carbonic anhydrase (BCA) at 298 and 308 K. Binding thermodynamics were characterized by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), while quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) was employed to probe ligand-induced changes in protein dynamics. ITC measurements in D2O were complemented by measurements in H2O over 288–318 K to assess temperature and solvent isotope effects. PFBS binds more strongly to BCA than 4FBS over the entire temperature range, whereas the thermodynamic parameters are similar in H2O and D2O. QENS-derived estimates indicate that binding of either ligand increases the conformational entropy of BCA. In contrast to the thermodynamic trends, however, the dynamic response depends strongly on the ligand: the diffusion coefficient associated with localized internal motions decreases with increasing temperature for the BCA-PFBS complex but increases for BCA-4FBS, indicating that the two ligands modulate the protein energy landscape in distinct ways. Despite their closely related structures, PFBS and 4FBS exhibit markedly different temperature-dependent effects on BCA dynamics. Our results show that subtle changes in ligand chemistry can reshape the balance between protein flexibility, hydration, and binding thermodynamics.

item.title: DC Magnetron-Generated Reactive Glow Discharge Plasma Activation of Acid-Etched Titanium for Superhydrophilic TiO 2 -Rich Surfaces
item.description:
Abstract
This study addresses the need for controllable physicochemical activation routes for titanium surfaces by developing a hybrid treatment that combines hydrofluoric acid (HF) microtexturing with reactive glow discharge plasma (GDP) generated in a DC magnetron sputtering (DC-MS) system, applied to commercially pure grade 1 titanium. Sequential acid etching induced controlled microstructural roughening, followed by a 1 min plasma exposure in air at 6 × 10–1 Pa to modify the near-surface oxide chemistry while preserving the etched morphology. Acid treatment preferentially dissolved the α-Ti matrix along grain boundaries, producing band-like corrosion grooves and hierarchical microtexturing, whereas plasma activation induced localized oxidation and produced a superhydrophilic response. Eight activation cycles over 150 days of ambient storage repeatedly restored the hydrophilic state, which persisted approximately 16 h per cycle. Raw X-ray diffraction (XRD) and grazing-incidence XRD patterns remained dominated by α-Ti, with no resolved reflections attributable to crystalline TiO2. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated the formation of a TiO2-rich surface after plasma activation, accounting for 100% of the fitted Ti 2p area, with no detectable F 1s signal. Adsorbed oxygen-containing species accounted for 4.7%, compared with 4.3% for the etched and 17.4% for the cleaned control. Because biological responses were not evaluated, these physicochemical changes should not be interpreted as direct evidence of improved protein adsorption, cellular behavior, bacterial resistance, or in vivo performance. This approach establishes DC-MS-generated GDP activation as a rapid route for titanium surface activation and advanced surface-engineering applications.

item.title: Comparative Study of Properties and Cytotoxicity of Eco-Friendly AgInS 2 , CuInS 2 , and ZnIn 2 S 4 Quantum Dots under a Unified Experimental Framework
item.description:
Abstract
Ternary quantum dots (TQDs) are promising cadmium-free nanomaterials for optoelectronic and biomedical applications; however, systematic comparisons among AgInS2 (AIS), CuInS2 (CIS), and ZnIn2S4 (ZIS) quantum dots remain limited because these materials are typically investigated using different synthetic protocols and characterization methodologies. Herein, we present a systematic comparative study of aqueously synthesized AIS, CIS, and ZIS quantum dots, enabling direct comparison of their optical, electrochemical, surface, and biological properties within a unified comparative framework. The nanocrystals exhibited similar sizes (4–6 nm), ensuring that the observed differences primarily reflected composition. Combined optical and electrochemical analyses revealed consistent trends in bandgap energies that were in good agreement with Mulliken electronegativity-based predictions. Despite their structural similarity, AIS showed long lifetimes and moderate emission efficiency, CIS exhibits suppressed photoluminescence due to dominant nonradiative recombination, whereas ZIS exhibited fast recombination dynamics associated with surface-dominated states. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy established a direct relationship between composition, defect states, and electronic structure, while all QDs exhibited high cell viability (>90%), confirming their cytocompatibility. Overall, this unified comparative approach demonstrates that cation identity governs band alignment, recombination pathways, and cytocompatibility, providing practical guidance for the rational design of cadmium-free quantum dots for photocatalytic, optoelectronic, and biomedical applications.

item.title: USP Standards for Dietary Ingredients Derived from Mate and Guayusa Leaves: A Quality by Design Approach to Method Development and Validation for the Simultaneous Determination of Methylxanthines and Hydroxycinnamoylquinic Acids
item.description:
Abstract
Mate (or yerba mate, Ilex paraguariensis) and guayusa (Ilex guayusa), both members of the Aquifoliaceae family and traditionally consumed as herbal teas in South America, are rich in methylxanthines and hydroxycinnamoylquinic acids that may provide stimulant and antioxidant properties for use in beverages and dietary supplements. This work demonstrates an analytical quality-by-design (AQbD) approach to developing a UHPLC method and sample preparation procedure for the simultaneous quantification of these compounds in mate and guayusa leaves and their extracts. Using AQbD principles, critical method attributes and parameters were defined and optimized through design of experiments to understand variable interactions, establish robustness within the method operable design region, and experimentally confirm the selected conditions. The resulting UHPLC-DAD method separates three methylxanthines and nine hydroxycinnamoylquinic acids within 12 min and was validated per ICH and USP <1225> guidelines, demonstrating specificity, linearity, precision, accuracy, robustness, and reliable relative response factors. Overall, the AQbD framework enabled the development of a robust method suitable for determining these analytes in a variety of dietary ingredients derived from Mate and Guayusa leaves.

item.title: Electrical and Thermal Transport in CaCO 3 Graphene Nanocomposites Derived from Oyster Shell Waste
item.description:
Abstract
Waste oyster shells provide a calcium carbonate, as Mg-calcite, feedstock for functional mineral composites. Here, shell-derived biogenic calcium carbonate (BCC) and few-layer graphene (FLG; nominally 1, 5, 7, and 10 wt % relative to BCC) were processed by aqueous planetary ball milling with Pluronic P123. Microscopy, diffraction, spectroscopy, thermogravimetry, and transport measurements were combined to examine the resulting powders and pressed pellets. Mg-calcite nanocrystallites and graphene sheets coexisted within micrometer-scale aggregates, with mineral particles preferentially observed near sheet edges. At 25 °C, the thermal conductivity of the 10 wt % formulation was 0.516 W·m–1·K–1, compared with 0.194 W·m–1·K–1 for the dry-milled shell. This approximately 166% reference-to-composite difference combines changes in composition and processing and cannot be assigned to FLG addition alone. Stable electrical measurements were obtained from 5 wt % FLG; the reported resistivity of the 10 wt % formulation was approximately 0.50 Ω·cm. The shell organic matrix may contribute to interfacial interactions, although its effect cannot be distinguished from those of Pluronic and processing in the present experiments. The observed transport differences among the prepared formulations provide a basis for future studies using matched processing controls to clarify the contribution of each constituent.

item.title: Photothermal-Augmented Cascade Catalysis: Engineering Nanozymes for Tumor ROS Burst Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Nanozyme-based catalytic therapy triggered by tumor-specific endogenous stimuli is an emerging tumor therapy that has attracted significant attention. Nevertheless, the efficacy of current catalytic therapies is severely limited by the intrinsic catalytic efficiency of nanozymes and the low concentration of endogenous substrates. Herein, a novel and efficient CuS-COF@PDA/Apt-A/GOx (Cu-CPAG) nanozyme was rationally designed with multiple enzyme-like catalytic activities and an augmented photothermal effect. Meanwhile, the nanozyme could ingeniously bind to the overexpressed MUC1 protein in MCF-7 cells, thus effectively addressing the critical limitations of conventional catalytic therapy. Following targeted internalization, glucose oxidase (GOx) within the nanozyme catalyzes the oxidation of glucose to elevate endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) levels in tumor cells and trigger a cellular starvation effect. Then, the accumulated H2O2 is subsequently converted by CuS NPs into highly cytotoxic hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which significantly promotes the intracellular accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in a cascade manner. Notably, owing to the excellent photothermal properties of CuS NPs and polydopamine (PDA), near-infrared laser irradiation exerts a distinct photothermal-augmented effect to further enhance the overall catalytic efficiency of the nanozyme, thereby inducing an amplified ROS burst in tumor cells. Consequently, the designed Cu-CPAG nanozyme can disrupt redox homeostasis in the tumor region through a photothermal-augmented cascade reaction, effectively overcoming the shortcomings of traditional nanozyme catalytic therapy. This work develops a promising strategy for cascade catalytic tumor therapy and provides valuable insights for the advancement of future biomedical applications.

item.title: Highly Luminescent Alkyl- and Alkoxy-Terminated Silicon Quantum Dots via Aging Following Single-Step Plasma Synthesis and Functionalization
item.description:
Abstract
Nonthermal plasma synthesis enables the continuous production and immediate surface functionalization of silicon quantum dots (Si QDs) in a single, flow-through reactor. While this process occurs on a millisecond time scale, the resulting nanocrystals are often limited by low photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY) due to persistent surface defects. In this work, we demonstrate that a minimal post-treatment, aging the Si QDs in specific solvents, can enhance the PLQY to ∼50%, approaching the performance of much more complex solution-phase methods. We find that the choice of the surface ligand and solvent is critical: hexanol-terminated Si QDs exhibit significantly higher initial and final PLQYs than decene-terminated particles, likely due to the faster reaction of alcohols with electrophilic surface sites in the gas phase. Among the solvents investigated, chloroform consistently yields the highest PLQY. Furthermore, we show that light irradiation at 400 and 633 nm drastically accelerates the Si QD aging process, reducing the aging time from hundreds of hours to under 20 h. This practical “synthesize and forget” strategy offers an efficient pathway for optimizing high-PLQY Si QDs for applications in optoelectronics and bioimaging.

item.title: Effect of Low-Frequency Pulsating Water Injection Parameters on Coal Permeability: Quantitative Characterization Experiments and a Field Case Study
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient stimulation of coal reservoirs is crucial for enhancing coalbed methane (CBM) well productivity. As an emerging unconventional stimulation technology, low-frequency pulsating water injection (LF-PWI) has attracted widespread attention for its ability to transform the pore-fracture system of coal reservoirs and its potential for engineering application. In this study, LF-PWI experiments are conducted using NMR, CT, and a triaxial apparatus to investigate the influence of LF-PWI parameters on pore-fracture properties of coal samples. The dynamic gray relational analysis (DGRA) method is employed to quantitatively evaluate the correlations of pore-fracture properties with porosity and permeability, respectively. Finally, the stimulation mechanism of productivity is elucidated and validated through a case study. The results demonstrate that LF-PWI can reduce the coal elastic modulus by 35.15%. The volume and connectivity of micropores and mesopores fluctuate, while macropores with diameters of 200–300 μm increase significantly, forming dominant flow pathways (>500 μm). Permeability continuously increases due to macropore development (k/k0 = 4.07). Porosity initially shows a rapid rise driven by macropore expansion (φ/φ0 peaks near 1.05); it then declines (by up to 9.95%) and gradually recovers toward unity as the micropores vary. Increasing the pressure amplitude simultaneously enhances the deterioration of mechanical properties, the fluctuation of porosity, and the improvement of permeability. A segmented control strategy employing high–medium–high pressure amplitude can help balance the pore-fracture network, preserve the gas source, and expand gas seepage pathways. Field application in the DFZ-1 well confirmed that LF-PWI mitigates coal fines flowback and increases cumulative gas production by 17.07%. This study provides a theoretical basis for employing LF-PWI to improve CBM well productivity.

item.title: Oblique Back-Illumination Microscopy Enables Phase-Gradient Optical Sensing of Malaria-Induced Intracellular Heterogeneity
item.description:
Abstract
Malaria remains a major global health burden, with diagnosis often relying on ex vivo analysis of infected red blood cells (RBCs), which incompletely samples key stages of parasite development. In particular, early ring-stage parasites exhibit subtle structural perturbations, while a significant fraction of parasite burden─including immature gametocytes─is sequestered within the microvasculature and is not readily captured in peripheral blood smears. Here, we present a label-free imaging and analysis framework that integrates oblique back-illumination microscopy (OBM) with data-driven classification to detect malaria infection by sensing parasite-induced intracellular heterogeneity. Unlike stained brightfield microscopy and quantitative phase imaging (QPI) methods that depend on interferometric acquisition and phase reconstruction, OBM directly converts intracellular refractive-index gradients into measurable intensity variations through noninterferometric phase-gradient contrast. By exploiting multiply scattered illumination and asymmetric detection, OBM enhances sensitivity to parasite-induced refractive-index gradients associated with Plasmodium falciparum development, capturing morphological complexity across the intraerythrocytic lifecycle. This enables the discrimination of uninfected cells, early ring-stage infections, and mature gametocytes. Fourier-domain analysis further reveals infection-stage-dependent redistribution of spatial-frequency content, providing a physically interpretable description of progressive intracellular remodeling during parasite development. Using synchronized in vitro cultures with brightfield validation, we demonstrate automated classification of infected RBCs with accuracies of 95% for binary classification and 82% for multiclass classification, with consistent precision, recall, and F1-scores across repeated randomized data splits. Together, these results establish OBM as a scalable, label-free sensing strategy that leverages intracellular heterogeneity as a diagnostic signal while providing access to stage-resolved optical phenotypes that remain difficult to interrogate with existing approaches. By building on prior studies of in vivo phase-gradient imaging, this framework provides a pathway toward integrating OBM with real-time analysis for noninvasive and field-deployable malaria diagnostics, particularly where conventional ex vivo measurements are limited by parasite sequestration.

item.title: Acid-Modified Biochar/poly(arginyl-Lysine) Composite as an Environmentally Friendly High-Temperature Shale Inhibitor
item.description:
Abstract
High-temperature shale oil and gas drilling calls for effective and environmentally friendly additives capable of control clay hydration, shale dispersion, and wellbore instability in water-based drilling fluids. In this study, we prepared an acid-modified biochar (BC)/poly(arginyl-lysine) (JL) composite, designated JL-BC, via physical blending, and then evaluated its inhibition performance by means of linear swelling and hot-rolling recovery tests. Under treatment withJL-BC solution, the sodium bentonite (Na-BT) swelling height decreased to 4.49 mm at 150 °C for 16 h, while shale cuttings recovery reached 92.1% after aging at 220 °C for 16 h, results that outperforming those of potassium chloride (KCl), polyetheramine (PEA), 2,3-epoxypropyltrimethylammonium chloride (EPTAC), and dopamine (DA). Furthermore, the water-based drilling fluid supplemented with JL-BC maintained good rheological behavior, fluid loss control and inhibition performance after aging at 180 °C for 16 h. Mechanistic analyses revealed that JL-BC adsorbed strongly onto clay surfaces via electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding, thereby weakening the electrostatic repulsion between clay particles and reducing the amount of hydration-related water associated with Na-BT, which contributed to the inhibition of clay hydration and swelling. An environmental friendliness assessment showed that JL-BC was nontoxic and readily biodegradable, that it did not significantly increase soil heavy metal concentrations and promoted nutrient accumulation in wheat seedlings. Collectively, these findings indicate that JL-BC is a promising environmentally friendly shale inhibitor for high-temperature applications.

item.title: AOXP: An Integrated Framework for Antioxidant Peptide Prediction Leveraging LLM-Based Semantic Features and Optimized Physicochemical Ensembles
item.description:
Abstract
Oxidative stress is a critical driver of various severe diseases, positioning antioxidant peptides (APs) as promising therapeutic agents. However, their discovery is constrained by the limitations of low-throughput wet-lab assays and insufficient computational prediction tools. To address this, we developed Antioxidant Peptides eXplorer (AOXP), a deep learning framework that leverages multiscale feature integration for high-precision AP prediction. Unlike existing models that often rely on isolated sequence patterns or manual feature descriptors, AOXP employs a hybrid encoding strategy that synergistically fuses deep, context-aware semantic representations from the protein large language model (ESM2) with explicit physicochemical and sequence distribution features. We constructed an optimized MLP architecture based on a refined 2400-dimensional feature vector, which was systematically benchmarked among five architectures and four feature selection strategies. Comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that AOXP achieves competitive performance across evaluation data sets, achieving a benchmark AUC of 0.736 on test_set1_drop and a sensitivity of 0.878 on the positive-only independent Test set 2, significantly outperforming current mainstream computational predictors in both sensitivity and robustness. Integrated Gradients analysis further quantified feature contributions, revealing that ESM2-derived semantics are the most influential features for model prediction (by feature number), followed by hydrophobicity, polarity, charge, and solvent accessibility. To demonstrate its therapeutic utility, AOXP was applied to screen a large peptide library targeting the Keap1-Nrf2 oxidative response pathway. A computationally predicted candidate peptide, MGRRHRHVTDEDDEENLGGDDDDGDDDVYMYPADMHPDERHAYREAV, was identified and validated through molecular dynamics simulations, exhibiting superior binding affinity for the Keap1 Kelch domain compared to the native ligand. AOXP provides a robust and efficient framework for the discovery of functional antioxidant peptides (available at: http://aidd.bioai-global.com/AOXP/).

item.title: SMART-Assisted Fabrication of Engineered Pichia pastoris Microbiofactories for Stable In Vitro Antigen Production and Storage
item.description:
Abstract
The rapid growth of recombinant protein vaccines underscores the need for manufacturing platforms that are efficient, stable, and scalable. We present a biomanufacturing approach integrating bioengineered Pichia pastoris with sodium alginate bioinks using the patented Sprayed Multi Adsorbed-Droplet Reposing Technology (SMART, US20250288524A1) to fabricate uniform microbiofactories. Engineered Pichia pastoris X33 strains expressing the truncated Epstein–Barr virus nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1, aa 379–641) from the pPICZαA-EBNA1 vector were encapsulated and induced with methanol for antigen production. SMART-assisted encapsulation generated microcarriers averaging ∼50 μm in diameter with a postencapsulation yeast recovery of 87% as assessed by the Alamar Blue viability assay. Across three independent biological replicates, hydrogel-encapsulated yeast consistently produced higher EBNA1 titers than free yeast, corresponding to a 1.70 ± 0.37-fold enhancement, as quantified by ELISA and confirmed by Western blot. Following lyophilization, in a single-experiment proof-of-concept storage study, the microbiofactories sustained EBNA1 production at 392 ± 11 ng/mL over 28 days at ambient temperature (24 °C), compared to 154 ± 18 ng/mL for free yeast; the sustained ELISA signal at day 28 constitutes functional evidence of metabolically active yeast upon reconstitution. These findings demonstrate the in vitro proof-of-concept feasibility of SMART-assisted hydrogel encapsulation as an ambient-temperature-stable platform for microbial antigen production. This approach provides a foundation for future development of biomanufacturing systems that may help reduce cold-chain dependence, pending further scale-up and immunological validation.

item.title: Solvent-Free Synthesis of Highly Luminescent Solid-State Boric Acid-Assisted Carbon Dots for Stable and High-Contrast Latent Fingerprint Visualization
item.description:
Abstract
The development of efficient, stable, and environmentally friendly fluorescent materials for latent fingerprint visualization remains a major challenge in forensic science. Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as promising fluorescent nanomaterials owing to their low toxicity, tunable optical properties, and eco-friendly nature. However, their practical application in solid-state systems is often hindered by aggregation-induced quenching (AIQ), which can significantly suppress fluorescence emission. In this study, highly luminescent boric acid-assisted carbon dots (B-CDs) were synthesized through a simple, rapid, and solvent-free thermal process using citric acid, urea, and boric acid as precursors. Unlike conventional approaches, the developed method enables the direct formation of solid-state emissive carbon dot powders without requiring additional surface passivation, purification, or polymeric matrices. Structural and spectroscopic characterizations supported the successful formation of heteroatom-functionalized B-CDs that exhibit excitation-dependent photoluminescence and strong solid-state emission. The synthesized B-CDs exhibited a high solid-state photoluminescence quantum yield of 77.5%. The B-CDs showed strong short-term stability, retaining more than 95% of their initial PL intensity after 60 min exposure to 95% relative humidity and during short-term thermal treatment up to 90 °C. Long-term measurements showed approximately 57% PL retention after 5 days at 95% relative humidity and approximately 48% after 5 days of thermal aging at 50 °C, while approximately 92% of the initial PL intensity was retained after 5 days of continuous UV irradiation. The proposed solvent-free synthesis strategy offers a simple and potentially scalable route for producing strongly emissive solid-state carbon dots, highlighting their potential for latent fingerprint visualization.

item.title: Electronic Spectroscopy of Atomic Defects in Molybdenum Disulfide under Ambient Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
We present results of electronic spectroscopy experiments performed on individual defects in the prototypical transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) under ambient conditions by way of conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM). Data acquired in the form of consecutive, high-resolution current maps at various bias voltages allow the assessment of local conductivity and differential conductance as a function of bias voltage for individual defects, the effects of which range from single-atomic sites to several nanometers in lateral size. Characteristic behavior in spectroscopy data allows the categorization of observed defects into distinct groups and provides clues with regard to their chemical identities.
